articles.full_text:
पश्चिमी हिमालय में तेजी से बढ़ रहा तापमान, बर्फ पिघलने का बढ़ा खतरा; रिसर्च ने बढ़ाई हिमाचल की चिंता
एक नए वैज्ञानिक अध्ययन के अनुसार, पश्चिमी हिमालय मध्य और पूर्वी हिमालय की तुलना में तेजी से गर्म हो रहा है, जिससे इस क्षेत्र में बर्फ के सबसे अधिक नुकसान का खतरा है। रातें दिन से ज्यादा गर्म हो रही हैं।
HighLights
पश्चिमी हिमालय मध्य और पूर्वी से तेजी से गर्म हो रहा।
रातें दिन की तुलना में अधिक तेजी से गर्म हो रही हैं।
सदी के अंत तक बर्फ में भारी कमी का अनुमान।
राज्य ब्यूरो, शिमला। हिमालय को अक्सर एक समान जलवायु क्षेत्र माना जाता है, लेकिन नए वैज्ञानिक अध्ययन ने इसकी तस्वीर बदल दी है। 1901 से 2020 तक के 120 वर्षों के तापमान आंकड़ों और आठ वैश्विक जलवायु माडलों के विश्लेषण में सामने आया है कि पश्चिमी हिमालय लद्दाख, जम्मू-कश्मीर और हिमाचल प्रदेश मध्य और पूर्वी हिमालय की तुलना में तेजी से गर्म हो रहा है।
आने वाले दशकों में इसी क्षेत्र में बर्फ के सबसे अधिक नुकसान का खतरा है। जर्नल आफ अर्थ सिस्टम साइंस में प्रकाशित अध्ययन वल्नरेबिलिटी आफ द हिमालयन रीजन अंडर क्लाइमेट चेंज में भारतीय हिमालय को पश्चिमी, मध्य और पूर्वी तीन हिस्सों में बांटकर 2100 तक के संभावित बदलावों का आकलन किया गया।
शोध में बीआइटी मेसरा, भारतीय उष्णकटिबंधीय मौसम विज्ञान संस्थान (आइआइटीएम), पुणे और अशोका विश्वविद्यालय के वैज्ञानिक शामिल रहे। अध्ययन के अनुसार 1901-30 के औसत की तुलना में 2014 तक सर्दियों में पश्चिमी हिमालय का तापमान 1.06 डिग्री तक बढ़ चुका था। बसंत में यह वृद्धि 1.08 डिग्री रही।
वहींमध्य हिमालय में सर्दियों में 0.96 डिग्री और बसंत में 0.83 डिग्री तथा पूर्वी हिमालय में 1.09 डिग्री और 0.83 डिग्री वृद्धि दर्ज की गई। शोधकर्ताओं ने ग्लेशियर-बर्फ निगरानी, सैटेलाइट डेटा, उच्च-रिजाल्यूशन माडल, शुरुआती चेतावनी प्रणाली और सतत जल प्रबंधन को मजबूत करने की सिफारिश की है।
रातें दिन से ज्यादा गर्म
शोध की सबसे अहम चिंताओं में रात के तापमान में तेज वृद्धि है। पश्चिमी हिमालय में सर्दियों का न्यूनतम तापमान 1.23 डिग्री जबकि अधिकतम तापमान 0.87 डिग्री बढ़ा। बसंत में रात का तापमान 1.25 डिग्री और दिन का 0.91 डिग्री बढ़ा। गर्म रातों का मतलब बर्फ के दोबारा जमने के घंटे कम होना और पिघलाव बढ़ना है।
यदि उत्सर्जन मौजूदा ऊंची रफ्तार से जारी रहा तो 2081-2100 तक पश्चिमी हिमालय की सर्दियां शुरुआती 20वीं सदी के मुकाबले 7.18 डिग्री और बसंत 6.91 डिग्री तक गर्म हो सकते हैं। मध्य हिमालय में यह वृद्धि 6.71 डिग्री और 6.41 डिग्री तथा पूर्वी हिमालय में 5.82 डिग्री और 5.16 डिग्री अनुमानित है।
32 किलो प्रति वर्ग मीटर बर्फ कम होने का अनुमान
शोध के आधार पर ये बताया गया है कि बसंत में पश्चिमी हिमालय में सदी के अंत तक कम उत्सर्जन की स्थिति में भी 32 किलो प्रति वर्ग मीटर बर्फ कम होने का अनुमान है। उच्च उत्सर्जन में यह नुकसान 95.9 किलो प्रति वर्ग मीटर तक पहुंच सकता है। यानी उच्च उत्सर्जन पथ में बसंत की बर्फ का नुकसान कम उत्सर्जन की तुलना में करीब तीन गुना होगा।
क्यों महत्वपूर्ण है हिमालय
हिमालय से सिंधु, गंगा और ब्रह्मपुत्र जैसी प्रमुख नदियां निकलती हैं और इन पर करीब 1.5 अरब लोगों की आजीविका और जल जरूरतें निर्भर हैं। सर्दियों में कम बर्फ जमने और बसंत में तेजी से पिघलने से भविष्य में नदियों में पानी पहुंचने के समय और मात्रा में बदलाव हो सकता है। शोधकर्ताओं ने चेताया है कि पश्चिम की ओर ग्लेशियर झील विस्फोट बाढ़ का खतरा भी बढ़ सकता है।

Newswise — A new purple cooling fabric developed by Chinese and Australian researchers could help people stay cooler during scorching summer days without having to resort to wearing white.
The high-tech fabric has been shown to stay up to 6.2°C cooler than conventional purple cotton when exposed to direct sunlight, potentially opening the door to a new generation of clothing designed to keep people cool during heatwaves.
The breakthrough, led by researchers from Zhengzhou University and involving Adelaide University, tackles a difficult problem: making coloured clothing that actually cools you down.
Most passive cooling fabrics are white because they work by reflecting sunlight away from the body. But darker colours absorb more of the sun’s energy, making them much harder to cool effectively.
Purple is particularly challenging because the colour comes from absorbing green light – one of the strongest parts of the solar spectrum.
Adelaide University Professor Jun Ma, a materials engineer from the School of Chemical Engineering and a co-author on the paper, said the researchers wanted to prove that effective cooling did not have to mean giving up colour.
“We have traditionally had to make a choice between cooling performance and appearance,” Professor Ma said.
“Our research shows that we can have both. We can make a fabric that looks purple, but at the same time reflects most of the sun’s energy and releases heat very efficiently.”
The researchers created the fabric using microscopic fibres containing a purple material called a metal-organic framework (MOF) and zinc oxide nanoparticles.
Together, the materials give the fabric its distinctive purple colour while helping it perform like a highly effective cooling material.
The fabric reflects an average 87.6% of solar radiation, while also emitting 96.4% of mid-infrared radiation – allowing heat from the fabric to escape through the atmosphere towards outer space.
The results were striking.
In outdoor testing under direct sunlight, the purple fabric was:
The testing also showed that simulated skin covered with the new fabric was up to 8°C cooler than uncovered simulated skin during the day.
That compared with a 4.6°C maximum reduction for white cotton and just 2.8°C for conventional purple cotton.
Adelaide University co-author Yangzhe Hou, a PhD candidate in the School of Chemical Engineering, said the technology could eventually benefit people who spend long periods outdoors. “For outdoor workers, athletes and anyone exposed to hot weather, staying cool is not just about comfort,” Hou said. “We are interested in developing fabrics that can help manage body temperature without consuming additional energy.” Unlike many experimental cooling materials, the new fabric is also lightweight and flexible, can withstand significant stretching, and allows water vapour – including perspiration – to pass through.
It was also found to be highly water-repellent and retained its cooling performance after 50 washing cycles.
The fabric provided strong UV resistance and retained its optical performance after high-intensity UV age testing equivalent to about 108 days outdoors.
Hou said the research could ultimately pave the way for cooling clothing in a much wider range of colours.
“The long-term opportunity is to move beyond the idea that cooling fabrics have to be white. However, there is enormous potential to combine colour, comfort and cooling performance in the next generation of textiles.”
The researchers say the approach could potentially be adapted to other colours by using different metal-organic frameworks with different optical properties, creating opportunities for a broader range of aesthetically appealing cooling fabrics.
The research is published in the journal Small. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/smll.74745

- Rajasthan Weather: Alwar Receives Heavy Rain | Jaipur Heatwave Alert
Rain alert in 12 Rajasthan districts today:Alwar gets up to 3 inches of rain, Jaipur hotter than Jaisalmer and Barmer
- Copy link
The Meteorological Department in Rajasthan has issued a yellow alert in 12 districts, predicting light rain today. It has predicted that the monsoon in the state is likely to weaken further from 26-27 August. The weather may remain dry in eastern parts and western Rajasthan.
Earlier, the spell of rain that started late Saturday evening in Bharatpur, Alwar, Dholpur, Karauli areas of eastern Rajasthan continued till Sunday afternoon.
During this period, Laxmangarh in Alwar received 75MM (3 inches) of rain. The rain brought relief to the people in these areas from heat and humidity.
A (mud/unpaved) house collapsed due to light rain in Baseri, Dholpur. On Sunday, the highest maximum temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius was recorded in Sriganganagar. The temperature in Jaipur remained above 35 degrees, which is higher than Jaisalmer-Barmer.
Hottest cities in the state
Major monsoon updates
57 mm rain recorded in Kathumar, Alwar
Light rain was reported in parts of Dholpur on Sunday afternoon. Rajakhera and Saipau received 6 mm each, while Baseri recorded 4 mm and Basai Nawab 16 mm. Kudgaon and Sapotra in Karauli also received 1–2 mm of rain.
Between Saturday night and Sunday morning, Kathumar in Alwar recorded 57 mm, followed by Raini with 45 mm, Rajgarh 39 mm, Baretha in Bharatpur 46 mm, Nadbai 33 mm, Roopwas 25 mm and Sarmathura in Dholpur 23 mm.
Eastern Rajasthan sees more heat
While there was no rainfall in the western districts, temperatures remained relatively stable due to south-westerly winds. As a result, temperatures in Jaisalmer, Barmer and Jodhpur, usually among the hottest districts in western Rajasthan, remained below 35°C.
In eastern Rajasthan, however, temperatures in Jaipur, Pilani (Jhunjhunu), Sikar, Tonk, Jhunjhunu and Fatehpur (Sikar) were recorded at 35°C or above.
Temperatures may rise to 39°C
Radheshyam Sharma, director of the Meteorological Centre in Jaipur, said dry south-westerly winds are currently prevailing over most parts of Rajasthan.
He said most parts of the Jodhpur and Bikaner divisions are likely to remain dry for the next week. Temperatures may rise in the border areas during this period, with some cities likely to record maximum temperatures of up to 39°C.
Weak monsoon conditions are also expected to continue across most parts of the Udaipur, Jaipur and Ajmer divisions for the next week. However, light to moderate rain may occur in some districts of the Jaipur division, as well as in Kota and Bharatpur, between 25 and 27 August.
Weather conditions in major districts
Jaipur: The sky remained clear and sunny throughout Sunday. With no rainfall, temperatures rose, and heat and humidity increased. Jaipur was warmer than several western Rajasthan districts, including Jaisalmer and Barmer. The maximum temperature was 35.6°C, while the minimum was 27.4°C.
Kota: The weather remained dry, with sunshine throughout the day. The absence of rain led to persistent humidity. The maximum temperature was 34.4°C and the minimum was 26°C. The district has received only 291.8 mm of rainfall so far this season.
Sikar: Clouds continued to move across the sky throughout Sunday, with periods of sunshine and shade. The maximum temperature was 36°C, while the minimum was 24.4°C. Humidity was slightly lower.
Ajmer: Monsoon activity has remained weak for the past week. The lack of rain has increased the effect of heat and humidity. Clouds were seen in the morning on Sunday, but the sun came out later.
The maximum temperature was 33°C, and the minimum was 23.4°C. The district has received less rainfall than expected this monsoon season, which has also affected water inflow into its major reservoirs.
Udaipur: The weather remained changeable on Sunday. It was sunny during the day, while clouds intermittently covered the sky. The weather became cooler in the evening. The temperature fell by 0.5°C, with the day's maximum recorded at 31.6°C.
Jodhpur: The weather remained clear on Sunday, with a maximum temperature of 33.6°C and a minimum of 26.8°C. The weather is expected to remain clear for the next two days. Light clouds may appear thereafter, although there is no possibility of rainfall.
Alwar: The weather changed from Sunday morning, with light clouds in some parts of the district and sunshine in others. There was some relief from the heat compared with previous days. The maximum temperature was 34.8°C, while the minimum was 25.6°C.

articles.full_text:
Temperatures are soaring across wide regions of eastern and western Japan on Monday, topping 35 degrees Celsius in some areas even in the morning.
People are advised to take thorough precautions against heatstroke as the mercury is expected to rise further in the afternoon.
The Japan Meteorological Agency is forecasting sweltering conditions for many places as a high-pressure system blankets much of the country.
Areas hit by last month's powerful earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture are also experiencing intense heat. As of 11 a.m. on Monday, temperatures had reached 35.4 degrees in Kosa Town, 35.3 degrees in Kumamoto City, 33.7 degrees in Yatsushiro City and 32.6 degrees in Uki City.
Weather officials say temperatures will rise to dangerous levels across wide areas in the afternoon, hitting 39 degrees in Hita City, Oita Prefecture.
They are forecasting daytime highs of 38 degrees in the cities of Kyoto, Tottori, Yamaguchi, Kumamoto and Saga.
The mercury is expected to go up to 37 degrees in the cities of Nagoya, Osaka, Fukui, Hiroshima and Takamatsu, and 36 degrees in Kofu City and Fukuoka City.
The officials say the daytime high will likely reach 34 degrees in central Tokyo.
A heatstroke alert is in place for 31 prefectures from the Kanto region to Okinawa Prefecture.
People are advised to use air conditioners, frequently drink water and replenish salt and refrain from outdoor activities.
The weather officials also say atmospheric conditions will become unstable across wide areas from northern to western Japan due to humid air and high temperatures. Localized heavy rain accompanied by thunder could occur in some areas.
A front will pass over the Tohoku region, possibly bringing heavy rain mainly on the Sea of Japan side from Monday night to Tuesday.
The officials are calling for vigilance against landslides, flooding in low-lying areas and swollen rivers, as well as lightning and gusty winds, including tornadoes.

Britain is currently grappling with a violent atmospheric shift as a sudden cold snap replaces a recent heatwave, sending temperatures plummeting to -0.2C in several regions. This abrupt reversal has triggered travel alerts across the country, with the Met Office warning of frost, dense fog, and autumn-like conditions that could disrupt outdoor activities and rural transit.
The transition has been jarring for residents and visitors alike, as the UK moves from extreme summer heat to sub-zero overnight lows in a matter of days. While urban centers are maintaining slightly higher temperatures, the rural landscape is seeing a return to conditions typically reserved for late September or October.
Northerly Breezes Drive Temperatures to -0.2C Across Britain
The current meteorological instability is being fueled by a persistent northerly breeze that has stripped away the residual warmth of the previous heatwave. This wind chill is particularly acute along the UK's exposed coastal fringes, where the perceived temperature is significantly lower than the actual thermometer reading.
According to data from the Met Office, overnight temperatures have dipped as low as -0.2C. This sharp decline has created a stark contrast between the daytime highs, which remain near seasonal averages, and the freezing nights.
Regional temperature variations are evident across the British Isles:
- Cumbria and South Wales: Temperatures are expected to hover around 2C.
- Northern Scotland: Lows are forecasted to reach approximately 5C.
- Urban Centers: Major cities are remaining warmer, with overnight lows staying closer to 11C due to the "urban heat island" effect, where concrete and infrastructure retain heat.
Rural Frost and Visibility Hazards in the Countryside
While city dwellers may only notice a slight chill, those in rural communities, valleys, and sheltered landscapes are facing more severe conditions. The Met Office has highlighted a significant risk of frost and the development of thick patches of mist and fog, especially during the early morning hours.
These conditions present a dual challenge for travelers: the physical cold and reduced visibility. Open landscapes, hills, and farmland are experiencing a rapid seasonal shift, creating a distinctly autumnal atmosphere. For those navigating rural roads or engaging in outdoor excursions, the sudden appearance of fog can create hazardous driving conditions and complicate navigation.
This volatility underscores the unpredictable nature of the British climate, where the leap from a heatwave to near-freezing temperatures happens with startling speed.
Recovery Forecast and the Return of Warmer Air
The current chill is expected to be a transient event. Forecasters indicate that the temperature recovery process will begin on Sunday, which is predicted to be drier and more settled than the preceding days.
Looking ahead to next week, a gradual warming trend is anticipated. Starting Monday, warmer air masses are expected to move back across the UK, lifting overnight lows and increasing daytime highs. However, this return to warmth is not expected to be stable.
Meteorologists warn that the upcoming period will be characterized by "changeable" weather. This means that while the mercury will rise, the stability of the previous heatwave will be absent, replaced by a mix of sunshine and variable cloud cover.
Thunderstorm Risks and Unsettled Weather Patterns
The transition from a cold snap back to warmer temperatures often creates atmospheric instability. The Met Office has warned that from Tuesday onwards, the weather is likely to become significantly more unsettled.
As warmer air clashes with cooler remnants, weather systems are expected to push northwards, bringing a high probability of:
- Isolated Showers: Particularly prevalent along northern coastal regions.
- Thunderstorms: The combination of rising heat and increased moisture in the atmosphere creates a prime environment for electrical storms.
- Prolonged Rainfall: Some regions may experience extended periods of rain as these fronts move through.
For travelers, this means the coming week will require high flexibility, as a sunny morning could quickly transition into a heavy thunderstorm by the afternoon.
WXCharts Predicts Potential Surge to 29C in Southern England
While the official Met Office outlook focuses on unsettled conditions, alternative forecasting models suggest a more dramatic return to summer heat. Data from WXCharts indicates that southern England could see a significant temperature spike.
According to these models, temperatures could climb as high as 29C by Wednesday. If this forecast holds, the UK will have experienced a full cycle of heatwave, cold snap, and heat surge within a very short window. This extreme variance places additional stress on travel infrastructure and requires visitors to pack for multiple seasons simultaneously.
Summary of Temperature Fluctuations (August 2026)
Why This Matters: The Impact on Modern Travel
For the traveler, this sequence of weather events is more than just a curiosity; it is a logistical challenge. The rapid oscillation between -0.2C and 29C means that standard "summer" packing lists are insufficient. From a health and safety perspective, the sudden drop in temperature can lead to increased respiratory issues for vulnerable travelers and a surge in road accidents due to unexpected morning frost and fog.
Logistically, the threat of thunderstorms following the warm-up suggests potential disruptions to domestic flight paths and rail networks, which are often sensitive to extreme electrical activity and flash flooding. Travelers should prioritize real-time weather monitoring over long-term forecasts, as the current atmospheric volatility makes 7-day predictions less reliable.
Britain's weather continues to defy expectations, proving that in 2026, a winter coat and a swimsuit are both essential for a single trip.

Delhi on red alert as IMD warns of heavy rain, lightning; orange alert active for Noida, Gurgaon, Ghaziabad
Delhi weather: The red alert is valid until 2.10 pm, with the IMD forecasting heavy rain of more than 15mm per hour in affected areas across Delhi.
Delhi has been placed under a red warning till at least 5pm on Monday as heavy rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds hit the capital, according to the India Meteorological Department's (IMD) district-wise nowcast warnings.
The warning was first issued till 2.10 pm, with the IMD forecasting heavy rain of more than 15mm per hour in parts of Delhi. The updated alert is now active for all districts of the national capital.
Red warning for Delhi
The IMD's district-wise nowcast map, issued at 11.10 am, showed East Delhi under a red warning for heavy rain of more than 15mm per hour, along with thunderstorms and lightning. Winds of 30-40 km/h in the affected area.
The map also showed several other parts of Delhi under the red warning category, while adjoining areas are under an orange alert.
The updated map has extended the red-warning areas to the entire capital, with the IMD warning of heavy run.

Orange alert for NCR
Meanwhile, Uttar Pradesh's Ghaziabad and Noida are now under an orange alert, along with Haryana's Gurugram and Faridabad.
The capital is likely to receive multiple spells of rain on Monday. However, the weather is expected to turn largely dry from Tuesday, with the IMD forecasting little or no rain for most of the rest of the week.
For Tuesday, the IMD has predicted only the “possibility of” very light rain during the afternoon. On Wednesday, a spell of very light to light rain is expected at a few places before noon. From afternoon to evening, another spell of very light to light rain is likely at many places, while moderate rain is expected at isolated places.
From Thursday to Sunday, the IMD has stated that no rain is expected, with partly cloudy skies likely to persist.
The IMD categorises rainfall up to 15.5mm as light, between 15.6mm and 64.4mm as moderate, between 64.5mm and 115.5mm as heavy, and between 115.6mm and 204.4mm as very heavy.

Why Delhi may see a dry spell
Experts said the changing rainfall pattern is linked to the monsoon axis not remaining over Delhi.
“It is still fluctuating, and is mainly remaining at the Himalaya foothills. It travels slightly southwards during the night, and thus we saw some rain during the nights on the weekend. However, from Tuesday onwards, the city’s weather is likely to be completely dry, as the axis will move completely to the foothills. Due to this, we are expecting dry weather to remain till the end of August, and even during early September,” said amateur meteorologist Navdeep Dahiya.
Private weather forecaster Ashwary Tiwari also warned of intense but scattered spells in parts of Delhi and the neighbouring areas.
“Scattered heavy rains with loud lightning strikes, gusty winds up to 25km/h will occur in parts of Ghaziabad, East Delhi, Noida, Gurgaon, Delhi, South Delhi, and nearby areas during next two hours. The weather will remain humid and hot after the spell ends, and there is a probability of more such scattered events in upcoming 2 days,” Tiwari posted on X at 10:55 am.
Delhi rainfall crosses August average
On Monday, Safdarjung, the IMD station considered representative of Delhi’s weather, recorded 3mm of rain. Delhi’s monthly rainfall is calculated by adding the daily rain received at Safdarjung on all days of the month.
With Monday’s rain, the total rainfall recorded in Delhi so far this month stands at 246.3mm, around 13mm higher than the IMD’s long-period average (LPA) rainfall of 233.1mm for August.

Last year, Delhi recorded a significant rain surplus, with 400.81mm of precipitation between August 1 and 31. The city had crossed its August LPA on August 15, after 11 days of rain.

Heavy showers swept across parts of Delhi on Monday morning, bringing a sharp change in weather and prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue a red alert for several districts in the capital city. The warning covered parts of East, South and Central Delhi. The IMD said that Delhi was under a yellow alert the previous day, as it had rainfall between 8.30 pm on Saturday and 8:30 am on Sunday, but conditions intensified rapidly as monsoon activity strengthened. Waterlogging was reported at Kamla Nagar, Connaught Place and Ashok Nagar metro stations, among other areas. The sudden downpour overwhelmed the city's drainage system, leaving roads inundated and commuters stranded. Rising water levels in the Ganga have triggered erosion in several parts of Danapur, posing risks to life, property and connectivity. Authorities are working to maintain ferry services, arrange boats and ration supplies for cut-off villages, while coordinating with the Water Resources Department to contain the erosion.
Bihar Minister Ram Kripal Yadav on Monday said rising water levels in the Ganga have affected several areas of Danapur, with erosion reported at multiple locations and increasing the risk to lives and property. Yadav, who toured the affected areas along with officials and party workers, said the administration has been directed to ensure that residents in flood-affected and cut-off areas do not face shortages of essential supplies or difficulties in accessing safe locations.
"Floodwaters have entered several areas, including parts of Bihar. Today, I toured the affected areas alongside officials and party workers. Erosion is occurring at multiple locations, increasing the risk of loss of life and property," Yadav said. He said he had directed officials to make arrangements for boats in areas where road connectivity has been affected by the rising water levels. He also called for ration supplies to be provided to villages that have become completely cut off due to flooding.
"I have asked for arrangements to be made, such as providing boats and, in accordance with established norms, supplying rations to villages that have become completely cut off," the minister said. Yadav also said shelters have been established at some locations and instructed officials to ensure that these facilities are adequately prepared according to the requirements of flood-affected residents.
"Shelters are set up in some locations. I have instructed that preparations be made at these sites according to requirements so that the flood-affected people face no difficulties," he said. The minister further highlighted the role of government boat services in providing connectivity and assistance to people living in vulnerable areas during periods of high water levels. He said government boat services have been operational in the region for the past several years through the joint efforts of the Centre and the state government.
Meanwhile, Danapur SDO Anirudh Pandey said the recent rise in the Ganga's water level has resulted in erosion in the area. He said the administration was working to maintain basic amenities, including ferry services, while coordinating with the Water Resources Department to address the erosion. The flooding and erosion come as water levels in the Ganga continue to put pressure on low-lying areas along the river. Authorities are monitoring vulnerable stretches and taking measures to maintain connectivity and provide essential services to residents.
With erosion posing a particular threat to riverbank settlements, officials are also focusing on reducing the possibility of further damage to homes and other property. Kerala’s Onam mood is at its peak, but the weather threatened to play spoilsport, with a strengthening low-pressure area over the northwest Bay of Bengal likely to bring heavy rain to several parts of the state through the festival days.
THIRUVANANTHAPURAM — Kerala’s Onam mood is at its peak, but the weather threatened to play spoilsport, with a strengthening low-pressure area over the northwest Bay of Bengal likely to bring heavy rain to several parts of the state through the festival days.
With First Onam falling on August 25 and Thiruvonam, the biggest day of the celebrations, on August 26, followed by Third and Fourth Onam, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has warned of heavy rainfall in several districts over the coming days.
Eight districts are under a yellow alert on Monday: Kasaragod, Kannur, Thrissur, Idukki, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam and Ernakulam.
The alert will continue in three districts on Tuesday, while weather conditions are expected to remain unsettled in several parts of the state.
The timing has raised concerns as the state gears up for the high point of the Onam season.
Streets, markets and shopping centres have been bustling with festival activity, while families are making preparations for the traditional Onam feast and celebrations.
Public events, cultural programmes and gatherings are also scheduled across the state during the festival period.
The weather department has, however, not issued a rain warning for Thiruvonam at present.
Authorities are keeping a close watch on the evolving weather system, particularly as the festival enters its most important phase.
The rain threat is accompanied by a warning along the coast.
Fishing has been completely banned along the Kerala and Lakshadweep coasts in view of the possibility of heavy rain and strong winds.
The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) has also warned of the possibility of coastal inundation under the Kallakkadal phenomenon.
Waves between 0.9 and 1.3 metres are expected along the Kerala coast until 11.30 p.m. on Monday.
Coastal residents and tourists have been advised to exercise extreme caution.
Beach visits and sea-based recreational activities have been discouraged until the warning is withdrawn.
Fishing vessels have also been advised to remain safely anchored in harbours.
For Kerala, where Onam is as much a public celebration as a family festival, the coming days will therefore be a balancing act between festive cheer and weather caution.
The skies may be overcast, but the Onam spirit is unlikely to be dampened.
The big question now is whether the rain will allow Kerala to celebrate its biggest festival outdoors or force much of the festivities indoors.
